theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: Which order best describes the yearly performance management cycle in a public body?
options: Review, reward, plan, and then agree the new job description
Plan and agree, monitor, review, then reward and develop
Appraise, discipline, train, then set brand new targets
Reward, monitor, plan, then review the officer's file

questions.stem: Why should an officer's yearly work plan be linked to the unit's operational plan and the ministry's strategic plan?
options: So officers may ignore tasks that are not in their job description
So the appraisal can be completed without holding a meeting
So that the Permanent Secretary signs every officer's plan
So each officer's work clearly supports the ministry's goals

questions.stem: At the start of the appraisal year, what should a manager and an officer agree and sign?
options: The officer's leave dates and overtime claims for the year
A list of the officer's past mistakes to be watched closely
Objectives, measures, competencies and development needs
The rating the officer will receive at the year-end review

questions.stem: A statutory body's appraisal form has sections on 'objectives' and 'competencies'. What do the competencies assess?
options: How the officer works: behaviours such as teamwork and judgement
The number of years the officer has worked in the public service
The officer's academic qualifications and training certificates
The officer's salary scale and the date of the next pay increment

questions.stem: An officer's appraisal gives objectives a weight of 60% and competencies 40%. She scores 4 out of 5 on objectives and 3 out of 5 on competencies. What is her overall score?
Why should each point on an appraisal rating scale have a written description, such as '3 = fully meets the standard'?
options: So that managers need not give any written comments at all
So different managers apply the ratings in the same way
So officers can choose their own rating at the review
So each manager can change the scale as they see fit

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of a formal mid-year review?
options: To check progress, update objectives and agree support
To decide the officer's final rating for the whole year
To start the disciplinary procedure for weaker officers
To move officers to a new unit without any discussion

questions.stem: A manager at a parish council has an appraisal interview with an officer next week. What should she do to prepare?
options: Decide the final rating and write it on the form in ink
Ask the other officers to give their opinions of him in writing
Review the agreed objectives, evidence and his self-appraisal
Prepare a list of all of his faults to read out at the start

questions.stem: Where and how should a formal appraisal interview be held?
options: In the open office, so other officers can learn from it
By text message, to save both the manager's and officer's time
In private, with enough time booked and no interruptions
Over lunch in the staff canteen, so that it feels more relaxed

questions.stem: Which approach in an appraisal interview is most likely to lead to agreed outcomes?
options: The manager reads the completed form aloud and asks for a signature
The manager compares the officer with other officers' ratings
The manager avoids any mention of areas that need to improve
The manager invites the officer's view first, then discusses evidence

questions.stem: At the appraisal, an officer strongly disagrees with her rating and says the evidence is wrong. What should the manager do?
options: Change the rating at once so as to avoid any conflict
Listen, look at her evidence and explain the review route
Tell her that the rating is final and end the meeting there
Ask her colleagues in the office whether she is right

questions.stem: Why do public bodies give officers a way to ask for a review of their appraisal rating?
options: To keep the process fair and correct mistakes in ratings
To let officers put off their appraisal for as long as they like
To allow managers to avoid making any decisions themselves
To give the human resource unit more forms to file away

questions.stem: In one division, 18 of 24 officers were rated 'outstanding', far more than in other divisions with similar results. What does this most likely show?
options: All of the division's officers are now ready for promotion
The rating scale is too hard for the other divisions to use
The division has met every single target set by the ministry
The division's managers may be rating too generously

questions.stem: What is the purpose of a moderation panel that reviews appraisal ratings across divisions?
options: To give each officer a second, separate appraisal interview
To set every officer's pay increase for next year
To check that ratings are consistent and evidence-based
To replace each line manager's ratings with its own

questions.stem: Which evidence is most suitable to support an appraisal rating?
options: The manager's general feeling about the officer's attitude
Records of work against the agreed measures, with examples
Comments from officers in other units who dislike the officer
The number of times the officer has asked for annual leave

questions.stem: After the appraisal, what should the officer's development plan contain?
options: Learning goals, activities, support and review dates
A list of the officer's ratings over the past five years
The officer's leave and sick days in the last year
The names of officers who could replace the officer

questions.stem: In a public body, how should appraisal results usually link to increments, awards or promotion?
options: Every officer gets exactly the same reward, whatever their rating
Managers decide rewards privately, without any evidence
As the body's policy and rules set out, applied consistently
Only officers who are on good terms with the manager gain

questions.stem: A ministry needs all 40 appraisals in a department completed by 31 March. By that date 38 were done. What percentage was completed on time?
A new officer at an agency is on a six-month probation. What should the manager do?
options: Wait until the last week and then decide whether to confirm
Set clear standards, review progress regularly and record it
Treat the new officer exactly like a long-serving officer
Ask the new officer to confirm their own appointment

questions.stem: Which situation is a capability (performance) matter rather than a conduct (discipline) matter?
options: An officer refuses to obey a lawful and reasonable instruction
An officer tries hard but cannot reach the accuracy standard
An officer is found taking money from the cash drawer
An officer is rude and abusive to a member of the public

questions.stem: An officer's reports are often late and contain errors. No one has raised it with him before. What should be the first step?
options: Meet informally, explain the gap, hear his view, agree support
Issue a final written warning and put it on his personal file
Move him to another unit without telling him the reason
Report him straight away to the head of the ministry

questions.stem: Before starting a formal procedure, why should a manager look for the cause of poor performance?
options: To find a reason to dismiss the officer more quickly
To show the other officers that the manager is in charge
So that the manager can avoid writing anything down
Because unclear duties, training or health need other action

questions.stem: A formal performance improvement plan is agreed with an officer. Which item must it include?
options: A promise that the officer will be promoted afterwards
A list of the complaints made by the officer's colleagues
The standard required, the support given and a review date
The rating the manager gave the officer three years ago

questions.stem: How long should the review period under a formal improvement plan be?
options: Long enough to show real improvement, as policy sets
One day only, so that the matter is dealt with quickly
As long as the officer wishes, with no end date at all
Until the manager has found a replacement officer

questions.stem: An officer is invited to a formal meeting about poor performance. What should the invitation letter include?
options: Only the date, with no reason, so that she cannot prepare
The concerns, the evidence and her right to be accompanied
A statement that she has already been removed from her post
A list of the officers who have complained about her work

questions.stem: At a formal meeting under the poor-performance procedure, an officer asks to bring her union delegate. What should the manager do?
options: Refuse, because formal meetings are always held in private
Allow it only if the delegate agrees not to say anything
Cancel the meeting and close the whole case altogether
Allow it, as the policy and the officer's rights provide

questions.stem: Which principle of fairness must a manager follow before making a decision under the poor-performance procedure?
options: The officer must accept the manager's evidence without question
The decision must be made before the officer is told about it
The officer must know the case and have a fair chance to reply
The manager must ask the officer's family for their views

questions.stem: During a performance meeting, an officer says a medical condition is affecting her work. What should the manager do?
options: Seek medical advice and consider reasonable adjustments
Ignore it and carry on with the procedure as planned
Ask her to name the condition to the whole team
Tell her that health is not the employer's concern

questions.stem: An officer's work has slipped since a death in her family. What is the most suitable response?
options: Start the formal procedure at once to protect the standards
Tell the officer to keep personal matters out of the office
Give the officer a lower rating at the next yearly appraisal
Offer support, such as leave or counselling, and review

questions.stem: After a formal review period, an officer has improved only a little. Under a typical procedure, what might follow?
options: Dismissal at once, with no further meeting or notice
A written warning and a further, final review period
A promotion to motivate the officer to try harder
The case is closed and no records of it are kept

questions.stem: At the final stage, an officer still cannot meet the standard despite support. Which options might a public body consider, following its rules?
options: Only a public announcement of the officer's failure
Only a transfer to a unit that the officer chooses
Redeployment to suitable work, demotion or termination
Doubling the officer's targets for another full year

questions.stem: Why must every stage of the poor-performance procedure be recorded and signed?
options: To show the process was fair if the decision is reviewed
So that the records can be shared with the officer's colleagues
So that the manager never has to meet the officer again
So that the human resource unit can prepare the payroll

questions.stem: Who should normally see an officer's appraisal and improvement plan records?
options: Every officer in the unit, to encourage healthy competition
The officer, the managers involved and HR, as policy allows
Any member of the public who asks the ministry for them
Only the officer, with no copy at all held by the employer

questions.stem: A manager rates officers lower if they took maternity leave during the year. What is the main problem?
options: It makes the ratings harder to enter into the HR system
It means the appraisals will take longer to complete
It means fewer officers will ask to go on training
It is unfair treatment that may break employment law

questions.stem: An officer joined the unit in October and the appraisal year ends in March. How should the manager handle her appraisal?
options: Give her the lowest rating, since she was not there all year
Give her the same rating as the officer whom she replaced
Rate her on the period worked, with input from her last manager
Skip her appraisal and give no feedback until next year

questions.stem: An officer has exceeded all of her objectives for two years in a row. What should the appraisal lead to?
options: Extra work taken from other officers, with no other change
No action at all, since she clearly needs no attention
A lower target next year so that she does not work too hard
Recognition and stretching development, such as acting duties

questions.stem: Why should managers be trained before they carry out formal appraisals?
options: So they apply the system fairly, use evidence and handle hard talks
So they can complete the forms without meeting their officers
So they learn how to give every officer the very same rating
So they can decide the size of each officer's pay increase

questions.stem: An officer's three objectives are weighted 50%, 30% and 20%. She scores 3, 4 and 5 out of 5 on them. What is her weighted objectives score?
A unit's main objective depends on several officers working together. How can the appraisal reflect this fairly?
options: Include a shared team objective as well as individual ones
Rate only the most senior officer on the team's result
Leave all team work out of every appraisal completely
Give the whole team the lowest rating if the result falls short

questions.stem: Halfway through the year, a new government priority changes an officer's main project. What should happen to her objectives?
options: Keep them as they are and rate her on the old project
Remove all objectives and rate her on her attitude only
Revise and record them with her at the mid-year review
Wait until the year end and then decide what she did

questions.stem: Officers in a municipal corporation say appraisals are 'just paperwork' with no effect. What should HR and managers do?
options: Stop appraisals altogether to save time each year
Review the system with staff and link it to real outcomes
Make the appraisal form longer so it seems more serious
Tell officers that their views on appraisal are not needed

questions.stem: Why is the officer asked to sign the completed appraisal form?
options: To show the officer agrees with every word on the form
To pass responsibility for the rating over to the officer
To confirm that a promotion has been approved for the year
To show it was discussed, with room to note disagreement

questions.stem: Before dismissing an officer for poor performance, what does employment law, in general, expect?
options: Payment of one extra month's salary to the officer
Notice given to the officer by a single phone call only
A fair reason and a fair procedure, properly followed
The agreement of all of the officer's colleagues

questions.stem: Where should a manager in a public body find the steps of the poor-performance procedure to follow?
options: In the body's HR policies and the public service rules
In the manager's own personal notes from a previous employer
In a social media group for public sector managers
In the officer's original job application form

questions.stem: A manager tends to rate officers who share his background and interests more highly. What can best reduce this bias?
options: Ask officers to share more of their personal interests
Rate only officers who come from different backgrounds
Let the officers rate each other instead of the manager
Use clear criteria, evidence and a second-level review

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: What is the usual name for the formal yearly process in which a manager and an officer review performance against agreed objectives?
What one word names the set period during which a new officer's suitability is assessed before the appointment is confirmed?
What term names the behaviours, skills and knowledge an officer is assessed against, as distinct from the objectives?
Objectives carry 70% of an appraisal and competencies 30%. An officer scores 4 out of 5 on objectives and 5 out of 5 on competencies. What is the overall score?
What one word names the process in which senior managers compare appraisal ratings across units to make them consistent?
What one word names a case in which an officer cannot meet the required standard of work, as distinct from misconduct?
What is the term for moving an officer to other suitable work, often as an alternative to dismissal?
Give the three-letter abbreviation often used for a confidential counselling service an employer provides to help staff with personal problems.
A unit has 25 officers, and 20 had their appraisals completed by the deadline. What percentage was completed on time?
What two-word term names the principle that a person must know the case against them and be heard fairly before a decision is made?
What one word names the process by which an officer asks a more senior person to look again at a decision about them?
What one word names a step up in an officer's pay within their salary scale, often given when performance is satisfactory?
In a division of 30 officers, 6 were rated 'below standard'. What percentage of the division is that?
What two-word term names a formal notice in writing that an officer's performance must improve by a set date or further action may follow?
Three objectives are weighted 40%, 40% and 20%. An officer scores 5, 4 and 2 out of 5 on them. What is the weighted score?

essays.stem: You manage a department of 30 officers in a ministry. Plan the yearly appraisal cycle for the department, from setting objectives to the final review.
essays.modelAnswer: In April, at the start of the year, I would brief all supervisors on the ministry's strategic plan and the department's operational plan, then have each supervisor meet each officer to agree four to six objectives with measures, the competencies to be assessed and a development need, signed by both. I would check that every officer's plan links to the department's targets. Through the year, supervisors would gather evidence and give regular feedback. In September or October, a formal mid-year review would check progress, update objectives if priorities changed and agree support, with any serious gaps moved to the informal improvement stage. In February, officers would complete a self-appraisal and supervisors would gather evidence and draft ratings. Appraisal interviews would be held in private, with the officer's views recorded and both signatures. A moderation meeting of all supervisors would then check that ratings are consistent before they are sent to HR by the ministry's deadline. Development plans would be agreed from the results, and I would track completion rates and review the process with staff for the next year.
markingPoints: Agrees and signs objectives, measures and competencies linked to the ministry's plans
Plans a formal mid-year review that can update objectives and agree support
Uses self-appraisal and evidence to prepare for the year-end interview
Holds private interviews and moderates ratings before submission
Links results to development plans and reviews the process

essays.stem: Describe how you would prepare for and conduct a year-end appraisal interview with an officer whose performance has been mixed: strong on some objectives and weak on others.
essays.modelAnswer: To prepare, I would review the signed objectives and measures, the mid-year review notes, the records of work and any feedback from clients, and read the officer's self-appraisal. I would draft ratings with clear examples for each, both strong and weak, and think about the causes of the weak areas. I would book a private room for about an hour, with no interruptions, and give the officer notice. In the interview I would explain the purpose and the structure, then ask the officer to give their own view of the year first. I would recognise the strong results with specific examples, then discuss the weaker objectives calmly, using evidence and asking what got in the way, such as workload, unclear instructions or skills. Where the officer gives new evidence, I would consider it fairly. We would agree the ratings, or record any disagreement, and agree a development plan with support and dates. I would close on a positive note, complete the form, and both of us would sign it.
markingPoints: Prepares with objectives, evidence, past reviews and the self-appraisal
Arranges a private, uninterrupted meeting with notice
Invites the officer's view first and discusses both strengths and weaknesses with evidence
Explores causes and considers new evidence fairly
Agrees ratings or records disagreement, sets a development plan and signs off

essays.stem: An officer in a parish council's revenue section has failed to meet the accuracy standard for four months despite informal support. Describe the formal procedure you would follow.
essays.modelAnswer: First I would check the council's poor-performance procedure and the public service rules, and gather the evidence: the standard, the error records for the four months, notes of the informal meetings and the support already given. I would seek HR advice. I would write to the officer inviting her to a formal meeting, setting out the concerns and evidence, the possible outcomes and her right to bring a union delegate or colleague, with enough notice to prepare. At the meeting I would explain the concerns, listen to her explanation and consider any causes, such as health, workload or training. If the concern is upheld, I would agree a formal improvement plan: the standard required, the support to be given, such as training and closer checking, and a review period, for example eight weeks, with regular check-ins. I would confirm everything in writing, including her right of appeal. At the end of the period I would review progress fairly. If she improves, the case closes; if not, the next stage of the procedure would follow.
markingPoints: Checks the procedure and rules, gathers evidence and seeks HR advice
Gives written notice with the concerns, possible outcomes and the right to be accompanied
Holds a fair meeting, hears the officer and considers causes
Agrees a formal improvement plan with standard, support and review period
Confirms in writing with appeal rights and reviews the outcome fairly

essays.stem: Compare the handling of poor performance with the handling of misconduct, and explain why a manager must tell them apart.
essays.modelAnswer: Poor performance, or capability, means an officer is trying but cannot meet the standard, perhaps because of skills, experience, health or unclear duties. Misconduct means the officer chooses to behave wrongly, such as refusing reasonable instructions, lateness without reason, dishonesty or abuse of the public. Poor performance is handled through a supportive procedure: an informal stage, then formal improvement plans with training, coaching and time to improve, and only in the end redeployment, demotion or dismissal if improvement does not come. Misconduct is handled under the disciplinary procedure: investigation of the facts, a hearing, and a sanction that fits the seriousness, from a warning to dismissal for gross misconduct, with less emphasis on training. It matters to tell them apart because using the disciplinary route for an officer who simply lacks skill is unfair, damages morale and may not stand up if the decision is reviewed under employment law and public service rules. Equally, treating deliberate misconduct as a training need fails to protect the public and other staff. Some cases involve both, and each part must be handled under the right procedure.
markingPoints: Defines capability and misconduct with examples
Describes the supportive steps of the poor-performance procedure
Describes the investigation, hearing and sanction steps of the disciplinary procedure
Explains why using the wrong route is unfair and risky
Notes that some cases involve both and must be separated

essays.stem: Evaluate the use of moderation panels and forced distribution (a fixed share of officers in each rating) in a public body's appraisal system, and recommend an approach.
essays.modelAnswer: Moderation panels bring managers together to compare draft ratings and the evidence behind them before they are final. They make ratings more consistent between divisions, challenge managers who rate too generously or too harshly, and help officers trust the system. Their limits are the time they take and the risk that officers' ratings change without the line manager explaining why. Forced distribution sets a fixed share of officers in each rating, for example no more than 10% outstanding. It stops rating inflation and makes differences clear, which can help where awards are limited. However, it assumes that every unit has the same spread of performance, which is often untrue; a small, strong team may have good officers forced into lower ratings. It can damage teamwork, since officers compete against each other, and it may be seen as unfair and be hard to defend if challenged. I would recommend moderation panels with guidance on expected patterns, rather than fixed quotas, plus clear rating descriptions, manager training and a review route for officers.
markingPoints: Explains how moderation panels work and their benefits
Notes the limits of moderation, such as time and transparency
Explains forced distribution and its benefits
Evaluates the drawbacks of forced distribution for fairness and teamwork
Makes a justified recommendation with supporting measures

essays.stem: Evaluate linking appraisal ratings to pay increments and promotion in a public body, and recommend how it should be done.
essays.modelAnswer: Linking ratings to increments and promotion can motivate officers, reward good performance fairly and show that the appraisal matters. It also gives the body a clear, recorded basis for decisions that may be questioned. However, there are risks. When money or promotion depends on the rating, managers may rate generously to avoid conflict, officers may argue harder over ratings, and the development side of the appraisal can be lost. Budgets in public bodies are often fixed, so the link may promise more than can be paid. Ratings that are not consistent between units would lead to unfair rewards and complaints. Promotion also depends on readiness for a higher role, which a rating in the current job does not fully show. I would recommend a clear, published link set by policy: for example, an increment only for at least a 'meets standard' rating, and promotion decisions that use the appraisal as one piece of evidence with an interview or assessment. This needs moderated ratings, trained managers, an appeal route and separate development discussions.
markingPoints: Explains the benefits of linking ratings to reward and promotion
Identifies risks such as rating inflation and loss of the development focus
Considers budget limits and consistency between units
Notes that promotion needs evidence of readiness beyond the current rating
Recommends a clear, policy-based link with safeguards

essays.stem: Explain how a manager should take account of health, personal circumstances and workplace causes when dealing with an officer's poor performance.
essays.modelAnswer: Poor performance often has a cause that is not the officer's lack of effort. Before using the formal procedure, the manager should talk privately with the officer and ask whether anything is affecting their work. Workplace causes include unclear duties, poor equipment or systems, too much work, lack of training or conflict in the team, and the manager must fix these, since they are the employer's responsibility. Where the officer mentions a health condition, the manager should seek medical or occupational health advice, with the officer's consent, and consider reasonable adjustments, such as changed hours, duties or equipment. Personal circumstances, such as a bereavement, caring duties or money worries, may call for leave, flexible hours or a referral to the employee assistance programme. If there is any sign of risk to the officer's safety, urgent help should be sought. Information about health and personal matters must be kept confidential. The procedure may be paused or adjusted while support is given, but standards still matter, so the manager should agree a review date and keep clear records.
markingPoints: Explores possible causes privately before the formal procedure
Identifies and fixes workplace causes
Seeks medical advice and considers adjustments for health conditions
Offers support for personal circumstances, including the assistance programme or urgent help
Keeps matters confidential and agrees review dates and records

essays.stem: Explain, in general terms, how employment law, public service rules and the principles of natural justice shape the way a public body manages poor performance and dismissal.
essays.modelAnswer: Employment law, in general, expects an employer to have a fair reason for dismissal, such as capability, and to follow a fair procedure. It also protects officers from unfair treatment on grounds such as sex, pregnancy or disability, so the procedure must be applied consistently to everyone. Public service rules and the body's own policies set out the stages, who may make each decision, the notice to be given and the right of appeal, and a manager must follow them exactly, since a decision taken outside one's authority may be overturned. The principles of natural justice require that the officer knows the concerns and evidence, has time to prepare, is heard fairly, may be accompanied, and that the decision-maker is unbiased and decides on the evidence. In practice, this means warning the officer in writing, giving real support and time to improve, keeping full records and taking HR advice before any final decision. A manager who follows these steps protects the officer's rights, the public body's reputation and the decision if it is later reviewed.
markingPoints: Employment law expects a fair reason and a fair procedure
Protection from unfair or unequal treatment
Public service rules and policy set stages, authority and appeal rights
Natural justice: know the case, be heard, unbiased decision
Practical steps such as written warnings, support, records and HR advice

essays.stem: Explain how appraisal results should be used to plan an officer's development, and how the plan should be followed up.
essays.modelAnswer: The appraisal shows where the officer meets, exceeds or falls short of the objectives and competencies. The manager and officer should use this to agree two or three development goals, linked both to the current job and to the officer's career aims and the body's future needs. For example, an officer who struggles with report writing might set a goal to produce reports needing no major changes. Each goal needs activities, which may include a short course, coaching from a senior colleague, shadowing, an acting role or a stretch project, as well as the support the manager will give, the cost if any, and target dates. The plan should be realistic within the training budget and workload. It should be written down, signed and sent to HR so that training can be planned across the body. The manager should check progress in regular one-to-ones and at the mid-year review, record what was achieved, and change the plan if needed. At the next appraisal, the results of the development should be judged against the goals.
markingPoints: Uses appraisal results to identify development needs
Sets a few clear goals linked to the job, career and the body's needs
Chooses suitable activities with support, cost and dates
Records the plan and shares it with HR for wider planning
Follows up at one-to-ones and the mid-year review and judges the results at the next appraisal

essays.stem: A statutory body's performance management system is seen by staff as a paperwork exercise. Recommend how to make it effective.
essays.modelAnswer: I would first find out why staff see it this way, through a short survey, focus groups and a look at completion rates and rating patterns. Common causes are objectives that do not link to real work, appraisals done once a year in a rush, ratings that do not differ, and results that lead to nothing. I would recommend linking every officer's objectives to the body's plans, with a few meaningful measures, so staff can see why their work matters. The form should be simplified so time goes into discussion, not boxes. Managers would be trained to set objectives, use evidence, give honest feedback and handle difficult conversations, and their own appraisals would include how well they manage performance. A formal mid-year review and regular one-to-ones would replace a single yearly event. Ratings would be moderated and linked, as policy allows, to development, recognition and increments, and poor performance would be dealt with fairly. I would report results to senior management, ask for staff views each year and adjust the system.
markingPoints: Investigates the causes using staff views and data
Links objectives to the body's plans and simplifies the paperwork
Trains managers and holds them accountable for managing performance
Adds regular reviews and links results to development and reward
Monitors and improves the system with staff feedback

practical1.title: Prepare and role-play formal appraisal interviews and agree development plans
practical1.brief: The assessor gives your group an evidence pack for two made-up officers in a public body (for example a parish council's planning section): their signed objectives and measures, mid-year review notes, work records, client comments and self-appraisals. As a group, prepare and hold two formal year-end appraisal interviews. Give each member a named role: lead appraiser (prepares the first appraisal form with draft ratings, weighted score and evidence, then conducts the first interview), second appraiser (does the same for the second officer), officer (plays each officer in turn, using a brief from the assessor that may include a disagreement with a rating), moderator (compares the two draft ratings against the rating descriptions and challenges any that are not supported by evidence), and recorder (writes up the agreed outcome and a development plan for each officer with goals, activities, support and dates). In a group of four, the moderator also records. Weighted scores must be worked out and checked twice. Keep each interview to 20 minutes.
materials: Evidence pack and officer briefs from the assessor
Blank appraisal forms and development plan templates
Computers with word processor and spreadsheet software
A private room or screened area for the interviews
photos: The completed appraisal forms with ratings, weighted scores and evidence
The moderator's notes on each draft rating
The signed outcome, with any disagreement recorded
checklist: Took a named role and completed their part of the evidence
Ratings are supported by evidence from the pack and match the rating descriptions
Weighted scores are correct and were checked twice
Interview invites the officer's view first and handles disagreement calmly and fairly
Development plans have clear goals, activities, support and dates
Kept the officers' information confidential and spoke respectfully throughout
safety: Use made-up names only; do not discuss real colleagues' appraisals
Treat the evidence pack as confidential staff information and return it to the assessor
Keep the role play respectful; criticise work, not people
Stop the role play if anyone becomes upset, and tell the assessor

practical2.title: Manage a poor-performance case through the formal stage
practical2.brief: The assessor gives your group a case file about a made-up officer in a government agency whose work has stayed below standard after informal support: the standard, three months of records, notes of informal meetings and an extract of the agency's poor-performance procedure. As a group, take the case through the formal stage. Give each member a named role: case manager (checks the procedure, sums up the evidence in a one-page case summary and chairs the formal meeting), HR adviser (checks every step against the procedure and advises the case manager, including on health or personal causes), letter writer (writes the invitation letter with the concerns, possible outcomes and the right to be accompanied, and the outcome letter with the appeal route), officer (plays the officer, using a brief from the assessor), and representative (plays the officer's union delegate or colleague). In a group of four, the HR adviser also writes the letters. After the meeting, the group agrees a formal improvement plan with the standard, support and review period.
materials: Case file, procedure extract and role briefs from the assessor
Computers with word processor software and a printer
A private room or screened area for the meeting
photos: The one-page case summary with the evidence
The formal meeting in progress, showing the officer and representative present
The HR adviser's checklist of procedure steps
The improvement plan and the outcome letter with the appeal route
checklist: Took a named role and completed their part of the evidence
Case summary is factual and based on the records
Invitation letter states the concerns, possible outcomes and the right to be accompanied
